label: Temple Scroll 11Q19 (Megillat HaMikdash) — Part 1 — Col 1–22
summary_plain: The Temple Scroll is the longest of the Dead Sea Scrolls. YHWH speaks in the first person — I will consecrate my Temple, I will dwell among them forever. The scroll describes an ideal Temple with three concentric courts: the inner court for priests, the middle court for males over twenty, and the outer court for all Yisra’el. Detailed instructions are given for the altar, the laver, the stairhouse, and the chambers. The festival calendar prescribes additional festivals not found in the Masoretic Torah: a Festival of New Wine, a Festival of New Oil, and a Festival of Wood Offering. The text rewrites Devarim as direct divine speech.
summary_scholarly: The Temple Scroll (11Q19 — Megillat HaMikdash) was acquired from Bethlehem antiquities dealers and is the longest Dead Sea Scroll at over 8 meters. It was edited by Yigael Yadin and published in 1977. Columns 1-22 cover the festival calendar and the inner Temple architecture. The scroll’s most distinctive feature is its first-person divine voice: where the Torah reports YHWH’s speech through Moshe (‘YHWH said to Moshe’), the Temple Scroll presents YHWH speaking directly (‘I will dwell among them’). The additional festivals (New Wine, New Oil, Wood Offering) are attested in Yovelim (Jubilees) and the 364-day calendar texts, confirming the Temple Scroll’s connection to the broader Qumran calendar tradition. The three-court Temple design differs significantly from both the Solomonic Temple and the Second Temple.

key_terms.definition: Temple Scroll — 11Q19, the longest of all the Dead Sea Scrolls (8.6 meters when unrolled). Found in Cave 11. Contains YHWH's direct address to Moshe describing the ideal Temple architecture, festival calendar, laws of purity, and the statutes of the king. Part 1 (cols 1-22) covers the Temple's sacred architecture.

The official Cave 11 manuscript designation for the Temple Scroll — the longest DSS text. Yigael Yadin purchased it from an antiquities dealer in 1967 and published it in 1977. A second copy (11Q20) also exists but is more fragmentary.

The Temple Scroll's distinctive literary feature: unlike all other DSS texts that quote or comment on the Torah, the Temple Scroll presents itself as YHWH speaking directly to Moshe — 'I command you to build my sanctuary.' This rewriting positions the scroll as equivalent in authority to the Torah itself.

The Temple Scroll describes three concentric courts around the central sanctuary: the innermost court (priests), the middle court (Levites and Yisra'elite males), and the outer court (women, resident aliens, those under purification). This structure creates a graduated holiness map around YHWH's presence.

The Temple Scroll specifies precise measurements for the inner court and Temple buildings — dimensions, materials, doorways, columns, and gates. The architectural precision reflects the community's belief that YHWH gave Moshe the exact measurements for his dwelling place.

key_terms.term: Four Gates of the Inner Court
key_terms.definition: The inner court of the Temple Scroll has four gates named for the sons of Levi, Yehudah, Yosef, and Reuven — the twelve-tribe gate arrangement that organizes the sacred space by covenant lineage.

The Temple Scroll organizes the Temple courts' gates by the twelve tribes of Yisra'el — each tribe has its assigned gate and position around the Temple. This arrangement maps the entire covenant community's identity onto the sacred architecture.

The central sanctuary of the Temple Scroll — the dwelling place of YHWH. The scroll describes its dimensions, its furnishings, its altar, and its inner structure. The Miqdash is the theological center around which all the Temple courts and their purity regulations are organized.

The Israeli archaeologist and general who purchased the Temple Scroll from an antiquities dealer after the 1967 Six-Day War. He published the definitive edition in 1977. The scroll had been in private hands for two decades after its discovery.

The Temple Scroll's inner court is flanked by staircase towers at the corners — a distinctive architectural element described in cols 5-13 that is not found in Yehezkel's temple vision. The Temple Scroll envisions a more elaborate structure than any previous biblical description.

faq.question: What is the Temple Scroll?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll (Megillat HaMikdash, 11Q19) is the longest of all the Dead Sea Scrolls — 8.6 meters when unrolled. Found in Cave 11, it was purchased by Israeli archaeologist Yigael Yadin in 1967 and published in 1977. It describes YHWH's ideal Temple: the architecture, courts, gates, purity laws, festival calendar, and statutes of the king. Part 1 (cols 1-22) covers the Temple architecture in precise detail.

faq.question: Why is the Temple Scroll's direct YHWH speech significant?
faq.answer: Every other DSS text — including 1QS, the Damascus Document, the Pesharim — quotes, comments on, or interprets the Torah. The Temple Scroll does something different: it presents itself as YHWH speaking directly to Moshe, using the first person — 'I command you to build my sanctuary.' This literary choice claims for the scroll the same kind of authority as the Torah itself. The community did not read the Temple Scroll as a human document about YHWH's Temple; they read it as YHWH's direct instructions for it.

faq.question: What is the tripartite court structure of the Temple Scroll?
faq.answer: Three concentric courts surround the central sanctuary: the innermost court (accessible only to priests), the middle court (Levites and Yisra'elite males who are pure), and the outer court (women, resident aliens, and those undergoing purification). This creates a graduated holiness geography: the closer to the sanctuary, the more restricted the access. The purity requirements intensify as one approaches YHWH's dwelling. This structure is more elaborate and explicitly organized than the Jerusalem Temple's actual courts.

faq.question: How does the twelve-tribe gate arrangement work?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll assigns gates in the courts to the twelve tribes of Yisra'el — each tribe has its named gate and assigned position around the Temple. This maps the entire covenant community's identity onto the sacred architecture. When the community gathers at the Temple, each tribe enters through its own gate — the whole of Yisra'el is architecturally present around YHWH's dwelling. This is not mere decoration; it is a theological statement about the covenant community's collective relationship to YHWH's presence.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll's ideal Temple compare to the actual Jerusalem Temple?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll's Temple is larger, more precisely organized, and more strictly regulated than the actual Jerusalem Temple. The tripartite court system is more explicit; the purity requirements more rigorous; the architectural detail more precise. The community saw the Jerusalem Temple as compromised — wrong priests, wrong calendar, wrong purity rules. The Temple Scroll describes what the Temple should be — a standard that the Jerusalem Temple fell short of. For the community, their covenant life was the authentic practice that the Temple should have embodied.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll relate to Yehezkel's Temple vision?
faq.answer: Yehezkel chapters 40-48 contain a detailed vision of a future ideal Temple. The Temple Scroll draws on this tradition but is not simply a commentary on it. The Temple Scroll adds architectural details (staircase towers) not in Yehezkel, reorganizes the courts differently, and frames the instructions as YHWH's direct command to Moshe rather than as a prophetic vision given to Yehezkel. The two texts share the vision of an ideal Temple but arrive at it through different literary forms.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yadin's acquisition of the Temple Scroll in 1967?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll had been in the hands of an antiquities dealer (and briefly visible to John Allegro in the 1950s) since before the 1967 Six-Day War. After Israel's capture of East Jerusalem in 1967, Yadin learned of the scroll's location and acquired it. This meant the longest DSS text spent two decades in private hands before reaching an institution that could preserve and publish it. Yadin's 1977 publication was a major event in DSS studies.

faq.question: Why does the Temple Scroll have such precise architectural measurements?
faq.answer: The community believed YHWH gave Moshe the exact specifications for his dwelling — just as YHWH gave Moshe the Mishkan specifications in Shemot 25-31. The architectural precision is not architectural fantasy; it is revelation. If the community ever had the opportunity to build YHWH's true Temple (after the restoration they awaited), they would need these exact measurements. The Temple Scroll is the building manual for the covenant's restored Temple — preserved until the moment it could be used.

faq.question: How does the Temple Scroll connect to the 364-day calendar?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll's festival calendar (covered in Part 2) is organized according to the 364-day solar calendar — the same calendar documented in 1 Chanokh, Yovelim (Jubilees), and 4QMMT. The Temple Scroll's ideal Temple presupposes the correct calendar: YHWH's feasts must be observed on their proper days according to the solar cycle. The Jerusalem Temple's lunar calendar meant it was celebrating YHWH's feasts on the wrong days — the Temple Scroll describes the Temple that would observe the right calendar.

faq.question: What is the staircase tower feature of the inner court?
faq.answer: The Temple Scroll's inner court is flanked by staircase towers at the corners — a distinctive architectural element providing access to the court's upper level and enabling the priests to perform duties at different heights around the sacred space. This feature is not described in Yehezkel's temple vision and represents the Temple Scroll's own architectural elaboration. It reflects a detailed, practical understanding of how the Temple's service would actually function in three-dimensional space.
